title: The soul and body (ST I.76)
hook: the soul is the form of the body, not a ghost in a machine

segments.voice: Yesterday, privation: for Thomas, evil is the absence of a good that should be there. Your line was a hole, not a thing. Which missing good did you name, and did you add a bit of it? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

"I'm stuck in this body." People say it on a bad back day, or in a hospital gown, or at the end of a long shift. The picture behind it is a familiar one: the real you is somewhere inside, a pilot at the controls, and the body is the machine you happen to be driving. Wear it out, trade it in. A modern phrase calls this a ghost in a machine. Thomas Aquinas knew an older version of the same picture, and in the Summa he takes it apart. Today: the soul and body, and why Thomas says they aren't two things at all.
screen: `STUCK IN THIS BODY.` → `A PILOT AT THE CONTROLS?` → `THOMAS TAKES IT APART.`

segments.voice: Thomas's key word is form. The form of a thing is what makes it the kind of thing it is, from the inside. An image of our own may help. Clay shaped into a cup isn't clay plus a little invisible cup riding along. The shape is what makes this clay a cup. Thomas says the soul is the form of the body in a deeper way: it's what makes this matter alive, and human, and you. So the soul isn't parked in the head, steering. Thomas says it's whole in the whole body, and whole in each part. On this view, your hands aren't tools you're operating. They are you, reaching. He has a second point. A person doesn't have one soul for growing, another for feeling and a third for thinking. One soul does it all. The same you that digests lunch is the you that prays. Genesis tells it with dust and breath. In the Douay-Rheims: "the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Not breath dropped into a container. Earth and breath, becoming one living thing. Thomas holds that the human soul is spiritual and outlives death. But in his commentary on First Corinthians, he says a separated soul is not the whole person. It's one reason the Creed speaks of the resurrection of the body, not an escape from it. And it's why Paul, in the Douay-Rheims, can ask: "know you not, that your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost". On Thomas's account, the body isn't the packaging. It's part of the person God made.
screen: `THE SOUL IS THE FORM.` · `WHOLE IN EVERY PART.` · `ONE SOUL DOES IT ALL.` · `RESURRECTION, NOT ESCAPE.` · then, large: `MAN BECAME A LIVING SOUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for your body as you. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet and move your attention slowly upward. Feet. Legs. Belly. Chest. Hands. Shoulders. Jaw. Eyes. At each place, don't treat it as equipment. Treat it as yourself. Notice where you've been carrying strain. Where it's tired. Where it's been ignored. Pick one place, and do something small and kind for it right now: unclench it, stretch it, let it rest. If you pray, you can thank God for one part of you that has served you well today. The bell holds the time.
The soul and body. For Thomas, the soul is the form of the body, what makes it alive and human, so a person is one thing, not a ghost inside a machine. Today's word.
Your line: you are one. Today, give your body one plain kindness, water, a walk, an earlier night, as care for you, not for a vehicle. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics profess belief in the resurrection of the body in the Creed, and Catholic teaching describes the soul as the form of the body, so that body and soul together make one human nature.

sources.work: Thomas Aquinas, Super I ad Corinthios

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: soul as the form of the body (I.76.1); one soul performing vegetative, sensitive and intellectual functions (I.76.3); soul whole in the whole body and whole in each part (I.76.8); the separated soul is not the whole person ('anima mea non est ego', Super I Cor. 15, lect. 2).
'A modern phrase calls this a ghost in a machine' (from the index hook) is left unattributed; it comes from Gilbert Ryle (1949), whose work is not public domain and is not quoted.
'An older version of the same picture' alludes to Thomas's arguments against the view he attributes to Plato (I.75.4, I.76.1); Plato is deliberately not named to avoid a foil.
The clay-and-cup image is the script's own analogy, flagged as such ('an image of our own').
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Genesis 2:7; 1 Corinthians 6:19.

Editor: framed the body claims as Thomas's account rather than the narrator's ('on this view', 'on Thomas's account'); softened 'that's why the Creed' to 'one reason'; dropped the 'whole question' count.
